newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasury builds delinquent debtor database.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasury builds delinquent debtor database.

text.p: The Treasury Department has developed a computerized database of people who owe the government money and is using private debt collectors and its own agencies to get payments, Treasury Under Secretary John Hawke said on Friday.

Testifying before the House government reform and oversight subcommittee, Hawke said most outstanding debt arose from failure to repay direct loans, defaults on loan guarantees and other forms of accounts receivable from government operations.
The debts totaled $252 billion at the end of 1996, with $51.3 billion delinquent because it was six months past due.
Hawke said that since passage of the Debt Collection Improvement Act of 1996, Treasury has made a determined effort to cut down on delinquencies by getting more payments.
"After all, every dollar that is not collected is a dollar that we will be responsible for borrowing to finance the federal government," Hawke said.
He said Treasury has built "a governmentwide delinquent debtor database" and is going after those who owe money by using its own financial mamagement service as well as private collection agencies.
Appearing before the same subcommittee, Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers said the tax-collecting Internal Revenue Service will turn to the private sector more to achieve its objectives.
"...The IRS of the future will have to contract out, outsource, partner with the private sector and rely on outside vendors to a much greater extent than the IRS of the present," Summers said.

He said it was impossible to eliminate the IRS since the United States taxes people on their ability to pay. Therefore, it was vital to ensure the agency works efficiently and that it was not made into an object of partisan political attack, Summers said.
